Disclosure: This article was written by me, an under-caffeinated human, with light editing and a technical review from Claude.

I was walking through a WalMart Supercenter with my kids the other day to pick up school supplies. We had a short list, and the store offered an almost unlimited selection. It was the perfect recipe for decision paralysis and overthinking. My daughter spent 15 minutes trying to pick just the right notebook design while my son got distracted by a rubber chicken that someone left beside an eraser display.

Overall, the experience was stressful, overwhelming, and a lot longer than it had to be. It also reminded me a bit of what it's like to find the right content on Substack. Tons of great newsletters are being launched and updated daily. But, aside from the bestseller lists and a few article recommendations from the Substack app, there is no really good way to search the entire ecosystem for the content you'd like to see and potentially subscribe to.

The inbox isn’t a library. It’s a landfill.

A few subscriptions are fine. A hundred and you’ve accidentally signed yourself up for a full-time job. That’s where Karen Spinner found herself, buried under newsletters she actually wanted to read but had no shot at keeping up with.

Most people just unsubscribe or let the backlog rot. Karen built a machine instead. StackDigest. A tool that chews through the chaos, spits out a clean digest, and makes discovery feel less like dumpster diving and more like actual reading.

Subscribe

She spent months on an AI writing studio only to discover her “ideal customers” were college kids trying to cheat on essays. Then came prototypes that barely worked, RSS formats that claimed to be “standards” but weren’t, and enough face-palms to make most people quit.

Karen didn’t quit. Frustration turned into fuel. Out of the mess came something that works. A personal life raft that became a product other people now rely on. StackDigest isn’t promising to save the world. It’s just here to save your inbox. Which might be the same thing.

# I shut down my AI-powered startup. What went wrong?

### Hint: It wasn't the AI.

Nov 07, 2025

113

72

22

Share

Disclosure: This article was written by me, a human, while winding down my latest AI-powered development project. The StackDigest timeline was created with assistance from NotebookLM, and Claude Sonnet 4.5 edited the whole thing.

I ran through my shutdown checklist for the last time this morning:

Delete production environment and data source: done.

Delete development data source: done.

Update code snippets on GitHub to avoid any use of Substack’s API: done.

Set up redirect for stackdigest.io: pending Cloudflare nameserver update.

Archive code, just in case Substack ever changes its TOS or begins a developer outreach program: done.

For those of you who are new here, I recently made the difficult decision to shut down StackDigest, my little one-person startup. And unlike the first AI product I built—the dearly departed Good Bloggy writing platform, which literally had no users except for me and a few crazy kids desperate to cheat on their essays—the StackDigest community grew to 165 users, many of whom actively tested it and even used it regularly.

And, while it had some bugs and flaws, it was a genuinely helpful tool.
